Bank and trading: the Bank page is read-only and shows cash, rent and the CRC in your Poinbase account. Poinbase's Funds page handles deposits and withdrawals; pick the coin first: CRC can go through the bank account or a wallet, every other coin only through a wallet. Depositing from the bank turns credits into CRC in your Poinbase account; withdrawing to the bank turns CRC back into credits with no screening (the Poinbase account only ever holds clean money). Withdrawing to a wallet needs a payee address and a few confirmations before it arrives; the gas fee is fixed at the normal tier and taken from the coin sent. A wrong address format or checksum is rejected; a correctly formatted address nobody uses means the coins are gone.¶Trading: PSC stands for Probably Stolen Coin, the coin mined by GPUs and miners. Poinbase spot has two pairs, PSC/CRC and SPARK/CRC, following the coin picked on the chart. Buys and sells are both entered as an amount of the traded coin; the preview shows the quote coin paid or received, the average price includes the fee and the slippage does not.¶The Web3 trade page can swap any two coins, always through CRC: with CRC on one side it uses one pool, otherwise two pools, with two fees and stacked slippage; the preview shows the amount received, the pools crossed and the loss. Stablecoin swaps (CRT or CRA against CRC) use stable pools: a {StableFee:%} fee and almost no slippage near the peg; during a depeg liquidity thins, and in a collapse it is pulled and slippage jumps.§Hardware wallets: on-chain coins sit in PLEDGER hardware wallets, each with its own balances and dirty coins (each coin tracks how many of it are dirty; see Taint). A wallet is an item: drag it onto the trading terminal to load it. Open it on the terminal's Wallets page; connect and disconnect at the top right of the terminal. Trading on the Web3 page and the shop and mixer on the Gray Net page use the connected wallet; with no wallet or no connection they are view-only and every balance reads 0. Coin-paying customers pay into the connected wallet.¶Payments (shop, mixer, Ponero desk, listing fees) start as an invoice on the terminal; type the payee address on the wallet and hold ✓ to sign. The last two characters of an address are a checksum, so a one-character typo is usually caught; once in a while it happens to be valid and the coins go to an address nobody uses. DEX swaps also need a signature on the wallet.¶Poinbase is a custodial account; deposits are sent from a wallet to Poinbase's deposit address (only PSC, CRC and SPARK; the compliant exchange takes neither the black market's CRT nor the Revolution's CRA, and the wallet blocks sending them to the deposit address; only clean coins can be deposited, see Taint) and withdrawals are started on Poinbase's Funds page. The Explorer on the Wallets page looks up transfers by address and shows only transfers that really happened: every movement in and out of your wallets (transfers, DEX swaps and other contract calls, miner payouts, withdrawals, coins others send you); Ponero is a privacy coin and never shows. More hardware wallets are sold by Dr. Jackson; drag one onto the trading terminal to add it, up to {WalletMax}. The shop has cheaper ones. A wallet you no longer want can be destroyed on the Wallets page; its coins are lost for good, and anything sent to its address afterwards is lost too.¶Transfers pay a gas fee: slow, normal or fast, and gas prices rise and fall over roughly a week; when the network is congested gas fees rise and slow transactions may be dropped from the mempool. Check the full address before sending.§Staking: CRA staked in the Revolution pool earns a daily rate that compounds into the stake; withdrawing means requesting first and waiting four days, with no interest while waiting and no way to take it early. CRA is partly collateralized: each CRA is backed by the CRC reserve the Revolution holds and by the balance token SPARK; reserve coverage and the collateral ratio are shown on the staking page. Interest is paid in new uncollateralized CRA, which dilutes reserve coverage, faster the more is staked; when coverage is too low the Revolution cuts the rate. The Revolution sometimes diverts the reserve, preceded by rumors: that is the warning. If coverage then falls below {CraCrashRatio:%} it collapses: CRA is worthless within three days and four days of unlocking is too slow; above that there is only a discount, and money from raiding the upper class slowly refills the reserve.¶Official minting: deposit CRC and SPARK (ratio per the current collateral ratio; the preview shows what is needed) to mint CRA, queued {CraMintDaysMin}-{CraMintDaysMax} days; the minted CRA goes straight into staking. Burning turns CRA back into CRC and SPARK, waiting as long as the unlock period; when the reserve is short the CRC share is cut by coverage. Queued mints and burns may be dishonored in full by the Revolution: the nightly chance is how far the CRA price is below 1 times {CraRugPerDepeg}; if the price is not below 1 it cannot happen.¶Staking accepts CRA, CRC, CRT and SPARK: the last three are first swapped into CRA on the secondary market at the going price (through CRC, with fees and slippage). SPARK's price swings hard and crashes with the collapse. Staking, minting and burning are contract calls and need a signature on the wallet.§Miners: RatDigg miners (M1 / M2 / M3) are standalone machines with far more hash than a card and a lower power draw per hash; they need a battery, take modules and use no rig slots. Only the shop's miner dealers sell them, gated by black-market standing (M1 {AsicRepM1}, M2 {AsicRepM2}, M3 {AsicRepM3}), sometimes second-hand. When one burns out, repair it by dragging electronic components onto it in order; it comes back {AsicRepairHealthCut} health lower. Somewhere between day {EraMin} and day {EraMax} a "miner era" arrives, announced in the paper a few days earlier: the big farms halve their power costs, network hash climbs, GPU miners are diluted and low-end cards barely earn, while miners still do fine.¶Payout address: each miner (rigs and ASIC miners) has a payout address set in its own window; its mining output is sent there every night in proportion to hash power, so two miners can pay two different addresses. It starts unset; with no address, or a wallet that has been destroyed, that share is lost, so change the address when you change wallets.¶Turbo boosters work on rigs and miners with the same rules as other machines: each use runs one extra cycle, which means mining one night right away. The cycle draws a night's power, its output is based on the current network hash and goes to that machine's payout address, and it counts one round of wear and sudden-death checks; the machine still mines as usual that night.§Perps: the Perps tab on Poinbase uses your account CRC as margin, up to {PerpPscLev}× on PSC and {PerpSparkLev}× on SPARK, isolated margin only, a single position at a time (never long and short at once); to add to it, top up the margin. Fills are worse than the quote (more so for bigger orders, like the spot pool) and opening and closing both cost a fee. Liquidation is checked only overnight against the day's average price: equity under {PerpMaint:%} of notional wipes the margin. There is also a nightly funding payment; when the price is above its 7-day average, longs pay shorts.¶Other traders' positions get liquidated with the market too: most liquidations leave margin that goes to the insurance fund, and the faster the move the more of them go bankrupt, with the fund covering the gap; after a big one-day move the newspaper reports how many traders were liquidated and for how much (your position included). If a liquidation loses more than the margin, the insurance fund covers the gap; when it runs dry (only an extreme, market-wide wave of bankruptcies does that) winning positions are auto-deleveraged and give up half their profit; anything beyond that becomes your debt. Debt grows {PerpDebtInterest:%} a day, is repaid first from CRC in the account every night, blocks new positions and cash-outs, and after {PerpDebtDays} days items in your shop are seized to cover it; whatever is still short is written off and the perp account is banned for {PerpBanDays} days.§Shop: coin only, no CRC, {BmPremium:%} above normal channels, with extra markup on high-tech goods and GPUs; the coin you pay takes its share of dirty coins with it and the goods carry no stolen tag; GPUs may be fake, inspect them yourself.¶Shop purchases: pick a seller on the left, the shelf is on the right, and after 'Buy' the payment panel sets quantity, payment method and coin. Each kind of seller takes different coins: hardware and tech take PSC and CRT; arms, drugs, chemicals, documents, luxury and personal sellers take CRT and the privacy coin; farming, husbandry, water and brewing take PSC and CRA; platform spot takes PSC, CRT and CRA. If you lack a coin the seller takes you can use the built-in auto-convert: it swaps from another coin in the wallet at an {BmAutoSwapSlip:%} slippage and signs once; or swap on the DEX yourself first, with far less slippage but an extra step. Listing fees pick a coin at payment time too.¶Shop cart: 'Buy' on a shelf adds to the cart; the floating cart at the bottom right shows the count and opens checkout. Checkout shows the cart on the left (grouped by seller, quantities adjustable, items removable, escrow or advance release for sellers that allow it) and payment on the right: each seller has a different payee address, so you pay seller by seller - pick a coin that seller takes, create an invoice and transfer from the wallet; or auto-convert from another coin in the wallet ({BmAutoSwapSlip:%} slippage extra) and sign once for that seller. Spot stock and merchant shelves restock every Monday and Thursday; other buyers also shop each night, each unit has about a {BmNpcBuyChance:%} chance of selling, and sold-out goods leave the shelf.§Orders and selling: Orders are cheaper than spot but take days and may be intercepted; merchants sell by type at their own price factor, {BmBulk1Count}+ items get {BmBulk1Discount:%} off and {BmBulk2Count}+ get {BmBulk2Discount:%} off, and a bulk merchant appears at random with large stock but {BmBulkDays} days of waiting; escrow costs {BmEscrowFee:%}, is released on delivery and refunded if the seller runs; advance release takes another {BmAdvanceDiscount:%} off, but a scammer keeps the money and only sellers with {BmAdvanceMinTrades}+ trades accept; the platform itself can rug, be taken over by enforcement, or a seller can be arrested, after which your orders get traced and crime logged; forum rumors can be warnings. An intercepted parcel sometimes turns into enforcement at your door: signing logs the crime on the spot and seizes the goods, refusing only costs the payment.¶Selling: on the shop's Sell tab, list contraband, high-tech goods and GPUs from storage at {BmSellMin}x to {BmSellMax}x the reference price. The higher the multiplier, the slower the sale (below {BmSellFastMult}x about {BmSellDaysFast} day, {BmSellDay1Mult}x about {BmSellDays1}, {BmSellMax}x about {BmSellDaysMax}), and the likelier and larger the taint on the payout, which also grows with how much you sold in the last 7 days; stolen goods taint the payout by their stolen heat (heat% of the payout coins are dirty); the Sell tab opens on your showcase of listed goods, and “Add listings” stages more: identical goods are grouped, the − and + keys set the quantity, the multiplier is picked on the left, and goods are listed only after you pay the listing fee with the Shelf button; all units of one item share one multiplier, so to change it take them all down first; up to {BmMaxKinds} kinds at once and {BmMaxStack} of each, {BmListFee:%} listing fee per unit; goods can be taken down from the showcase and return to storage, the fee is not refunded; “Accepted coins” on the showcase chooses which coins you take: every extra coin adds one more sale roll each night (in random order, with a different number of buyers per coin), so accepting more coins sells faster, and the payout arrives in the coin of the winning roll; {BmCommission:%} commission, payout held {BmSaleHold} days before reaching your wallet; a fake card may be spotted and returned, hurting your rating; if the platform rugs, listed goods and unreleased payouts are gone.§Prediction markets (Web3 Predict page, from game day {PredictUnlockDay}): each market is a yes/no question about things the game itself rolls or schedules: a news event appearing, a faction operation starting, tomorrow's water purity, the PSC price. A market is open until its window starts and settles on the night of the window's last day. Buy Yes or No with CRC from your on-chain wallet (a contract call: sign on the wallet; the position belongs to the signing wallet); the price is the market's implied probability and rises as you buy; each winning share pays 1 credit; {PredictFee:%} fee on each trade; each market has a position limit. If the CRC you staked was partly dirty, that share of the payout is dirty too.¶Rumor slips and faction perks can tell you ahead of time that something will happen; betting Yes on such a market is an insider bet. Insider bets pay out as usual, but the police suspect insider trading: at settlement or on sale, the payout for the insider shares is marked as dirty coins in the receiving wallet. If game data is missing for the window (for example you skipped the nightly settlement), the market is void and the stake is refunded.§Prices react to news: each night every open market moves halfway toward the fair probability given public information, plus some noise; so whoever reads the paper, a rumor slip or a faction perk first can buy ahead and sell after the move instead of waiting for settlement. The clue list in a market panel shows what you know about it: schedules, cooldowns, the halving day, recent gas values, the CRA reserve level, ASIC-era announcements.¶Patterns you can work out: faction operations are triggered by hidden power values at thresholds (for example a crackdown needs security >= 20 and black market >= 40, and drops security by 20); gas runs on a seven-day cycle; the price anchor ramps up the week before a halving; scheduled crackdowns and blackouts move the anchor but the market price does not reflect them ahead of time; the faster the reserve drains (the more is staked) the earlier CRA warns; the PSC price market can be moved by your own big orders. The intel broker (needs enough black-market standing) sells a situation brief (the five power values and what each faction can launch now, in CRT) and three grades of insider tip (only for faction operations and the ASIC era, which are already decided; accuracy rises with each tier; priced by market size; some tips are fake and say the opposite of the truth); betting the tipped side counts as an insider bet. Market size grows with the day and a wrong bet loses the whole stake, so do not put everything on one market.§Manipulation checks: your big Poinbase spot orders push the price away from where it would be without you (the push decays nightly with the price reversion; the market clue shows it). Once the push exceeds {ManipFree:%}, if you profit from the price (a PSC price market won in the direction you pushed, or a perp closed at a profit in that direction) you may be caught: the bigger the push the likelier (capped at {ManipMax:%}). When caught, the payout still goes through: a prediction payout is marked as dirty coins in full; a perp profit stays in the account and {PredictFraudShare:%} of it goes on record as fraud (up to {PredictFraudCap}); the paper reports the investigation.¶Short-then-dump is not a sure thing: perp slippage on both sides and the spot round trip often cost more than the short earns.§High-yield scheme (Yield page, Issue; from game day {PonziMinDay}, one per save): pick a daily rate ({PonziRates[0]:%}-{PonziRates[4]:%}), pay the marketing cost to launch (launching and rugging are contract calls signed on the wallet), and lower-level people deposit CRC by rate and lower-level standing; the higher the rate the faster they come. Each night interest is paid first from new deposits, then from the issuer wallet; if you cannot cover it there is a run and the scheme collapses; {PonziWithdraw:%} of the pool is withdrawn each night, and the bigger the pool and the higher the rate the likelier a report, which also collapses it. On collapse the pool is confiscated. You can rug the pool any time (click twice to confirm): it goes to the issuer wallet and all of that CRC is dirty (launder it before depositing to Poinbase). Rugging and collapse both put fraud on record and wipe your lower-level standing. The word-on-the-street line hints at the report risk.§Scams: wicks - some mornings the price is slammed {WickMin:%}-{WickMax:%} up or down at open; most of it reverts that night, but some are real; the perp mark price only takes half, so do not panic-sell into a wick.¶Airdrops (Web3 Airdrops page) - each airdrop needs the wallet authorized first (one signed authorization contract), then a signed claim; check the approval scope before authorizing: real airdrops need no approval or a small one of a few dozen; an unlimited approval, or one far larger than the reward, is phishing, often under a lookalike name (0 for o, 1 for l), and a night or two later that coin is taken from the wallet. Approvals are listed on the right of the Airdrops page and can be revoked with a signature, after which nothing can be taken.¶Third-party yield pools (Yield page, Deposit) - {YieldRates[0]:%}-{YieldRates[2]:%} a day; you can see the reserve, whether there is a timelock and an audit, but not whether it is a scam: the higher the rate the likelier a rug, a timelock and an audit make it less likely; an honest pool closes and returns principal when its reserve cannot pay interest, a scam pool can vanish any night. Timelocked pools take {YieldLockDays} days to withdraw.¶Forged transfers - a coin-paying customer who opens with "already sent, here's the screenshot, hand it over" never pays; honest ones say it takes a moment to confirm on chain.§Charts: the Poinbase spot page and the Web3 trade page can switch between daily candles of every coin (the perp page shows the current product, predictions show PSC), green up and red down; the yellow line is the 7-day average (perp funding uses it); the bars below are volume (grey the market, cyan you: spot, DEX, mint/burn, Ponero swaps and perp opens/closes all count). The bigger the move the more the market trades; wicks leave long shadows.§Story links: choices in the game's storylines change this market; the paper reports them the next day and the market takes a few days to react. Serpico's evidence to the Revolution: the CRA reserve is topped up, the collapse chance halves for {StorySecDays} days and SPARK rises {StorySerpicoSpark:+%} over {StorySparkNights} nights; to the black market: CRT depeg and sell-out chances halve; to Security: for {StorySecDays} days the mixer cleans worse (each round ×{StorySecMixClean}), and mixer sanctions and manipulation checks are stricter. Eleanor leaks the drive: the CRC custodian write-down chance doubles and SPARK rises {StoryLeakSpark:+%}; returns it: the CRC depeg chance halves. Officer Lun arrested: for {StoryLunDays} days manipulation checks are stricter and more OTC clients are undercover.¶Mixer operator Tumbler (after unlocking the mixer, from day {TumblerMinDay}): he visits a few times and finally asks you to hide a key drive. Hide it and give it back: mixer fees halve and the anonymity set grows, plus a gift; but the drive is contraband and goes on your record if a search turns it up meanwhile. Report him: a bounty and Security standing, and the mixer shuts down (coins inside come back). Sell it to the black market: a sum of CRT (half of it dirty) and black-market standing, after which mixer fees rise and the chance of a rug goes up.¶After Tumbler: between his second and third visits a Security agent comes to ask whether he has been to your shop. Admit it: Security standing +{TumblerAgentSecRep}; but if you then hide the drive for him, the agent searches the shop the day before Tumbler comes back for it, and confiscates the drive and records contraband if he finds it. If the key ends up with Security (you report him, the drive is seized, or you no longer have it when he comes back), the mixing records are rebuilt: {PredictFraudShare:%} of the taint washed off mixer payouts in the last {TumblerLeakDays} days goes on record as fraud (up to {PredictFraudCap}). A report leads to a trial: you can bet on the verdict in the prediction market, and the paper covers the hearings each day; if he is acquitted, he takes revenge. If you sold the drive, the black market pulls the rug {TumblerBmRugMin}–{TumblerBmRugMax} days later, every coin in transit in the mixer is lost, and he takes revenge as well. Hide the drive and give it back, and he warns you the night before a Security crackdown. {TumblerRebrandDays} days after the mixer shuts down it comes back online under a new name; some of these are Security honeypots, and every coin withdrawn from one comes back dirty. Be wary of a fee that looks too low.§Mixer and privacy coin: pick a coin, amount and rounds; each round takes a fee and cleans part of the dirty coins, rounds equal days of waiting, and the coins come back to the same address; the more you deposit, the worse the cleaning. During crackdowns the mixer may be sanctioned; payouts due meanwhile are not cleaned and come back all dirty.¶Privacy-coin swap (Web3 trade page, needs black-market standing): Ponero is a privacy coin and dirty coins swapped in simply disappear and the Ponero you get is clean; {PoneroFee:%} fee each way, and swaps in and out share a daily limit of {PoneroDailyCap} credits.§OTC clients (network upgrade "OTC Desk"): the Black Lamp gets one more target, OTC client (double-click the lamp to switch). It lights up only in the display case and attracts people like the original Black Lamp, by the number of lamps and your black-market reputation; the upgrade includes one lamp. Half of the clients want to sell you coins, half want to buy coins from you, always for cash. After the client states the offer, choose to talk at the terminal: the terminal opens the counter trade page while the client waits at the counter. You can take only part of the deal, at 25% / 50% / 75% / 100% or a typed amount, and the cash scales with it; choose Pass or send the client away to decline. Deal sizes grow with the rent.¶Selling clients: on a deal you pay cash and the coins go straight to the connected wallet. When something happens in the station the coins usually come from it: CRT during a gang war or crackdown, PSC during a Revolution raid on the upper levels or lower-level unrest, all of them dirty. Otherwise they are PSC, CRT or CRA at random, {OtcTaintMin:%}–{OtcTaintMax:%} of them dirty, and dirtier coins are cheaper (the asking price falls from {OtcCutClean:%} to {OtcCutDirty:%} of the value). The client does not say how dirty the coins are: the trade page shows his address, and Look up opens its history in the explorer; the more of it comes from the mixer, the black-market platform or scam addresses, the dirtier. Once the Ponero desk is open someone occasionally sells Ponero, which carries no taint but costs more. Now and then the client is undercover: taking the deal loses the cash and records fencing, more often during a crackdown.¶Buying clients: they may want any coin, and they bid the market price plus a random markup (from {OtcBidMin:+%} to {OtcBidMax:+%} of the market price); whether it is worth selling is up to you. On a deal PLEDGER opens with the address and amount filled in; sign and wait for confirmation, and the client pays cash and leaves when it arrives. If the client leaves before you sign, the deal is void. Coins you sell are not traced for taint.¶My mixer (Gray Net page, comes with the OTC Desk): fund it and open, clients deposit tainted coins, and after a few days they are paid out while you keep the fee. Each round washes off part of the taint according to the anonymity set, which is mostly your capital and uncollected earnings (client coins in transit count only partly), so more funding washes cleaner. Clients compare the fee plus the taint left on payouts with Tumbler's mixer and go where it is cheaper, and a higher black-market reputation brings more of them; Wash Efficiency is the share of taint recently washed off payouts, and higher is better. Fee earnings stay in the pool and are all dirty when you take them out; capital comes back with its own share of dirty coins. More traffic raises the heat (a bigger pool hides coins a little better, but it also draws more traffic, so overall it gets more attention), and with it the chance of a Security raid: capital, earnings and client coins are all confiscated, fencing goes on record, and the mixer is closed for {OwnMixSeizeDays} days. Now and then an undercover officer deposits on an open night, which also records fencing. You can pull the rug at any time: everything, client coins included, comes to you all dirty, fraud goes on record, black-market reputation drops, and the mixer closes for good.§Taint: in every wallet, each coin tracks how many of it are dirty (shown in the balances on the Wallets page and on PLEDGER). Dirty coins come from OTC clients who sell to you, coin-paying customers (by the goods' stolen heat), Gray Net sales of stolen goods, insider bets and manipulation in the prediction market, a Ponzi pull-out, earnings from your own mixer, the CRT from selling the key drive, and flagged mixer payouts. Taint lives only in Web3 wallets: spending, sending or paying fees takes dirty coins in proportion to that coin's dirty share; swapping carries the share over to the coin you get (60% dirty CRT swapped for PSC gives 60% dirty PSC); Ponero carries none. Poinbase takes only clean coins: each coin can deposit at most its clean amount and the dirty ones stay in the wallet; so the Poinbase account and the bank only ever hold clean money, and withdrawing to the bank has no screening, just a {ExchangeFee:%} fee. Sending clean coins into a wallet does not make the dirty ones clean. Ways to get rid of dirty coins: the mixer, the Ponero swap, selling coins to buying OTC clients (coins you sell are not traced), and paying in the Web3 shop.¶Before destroying a wallet move the coins out yourself, and withdraw positions and deposits first: whatever is left goes with the wallet.

Graphics cards are the core of every mining rig, and the goods most often counterfeited on the used market.
Four things show whether a card is genuine: fan count, power connector, back print and serial number. Only a card that matches its stated model on all four is genuine; any single mismatch means a counterfeit.
A card's value depends on the model of the chip inside and its health, and every sign of wear lowers the price.

This guide provides all the knowledge needed to appraise a graphics card.
The model sets the fan count and the power connector. A counterfeit is a low-model chip in a high-model shell, and its performance and value follow the chip inside.

The model sets the fan count: one fan on the RTX 60 and RX 70, two on the RTX 70 and RX 80, three on the RTX 80, RTX 90, RX 800 and RX 900.\nA fan count that does not match the stated model marks a counterfeit.

The model also sets the power connector: 6-pin on the RTX 60 and RX 70, 8-pin on the RTX 70, RTX 80, RX 80 and RX 800, dual 8-pin on the RTX 90 and RX 900.\nA power connector that does not match the stated model marks a counterfeit.
The serial number is on a sticker on the back, as prefix, model code, hyphen, two-digit factory code, hyphen and four-digit sequence, for example PB2-21-6251.

Model codes 1 to 4 stand for RTX 60 / RX 70, RTX 70 / RX 80, RTX 80 / RX 800 and RTX 90 / RX 900.\nA model code that does not match the model (the sticker belongs to the original chip), or an invalid factory code or length (a sticker added later), marks a counterfeit. The factory code only proves authenticity and does not change the price.
A card is genuine only if fan count, power connector, print and serial number all match. A counterfeit fails at least one, but may get the others right, so check every one.

Inspect with the magnifier. In the label bar, only the model row has a Point out model button; the four rows below it (fan count, power connector, back print, serial number) are read-only, and each of the four condition rows has its own Point out button.
Point out a hidden condition problem and that row switches to the true state and the price drops by the difference; point out something true and the other side refuses and your reputation suffers.
If any of the four proof rows does not match the stated model, point out the model: the card is then ruled a counterfeit, the model reverts to the real chip, and the price is recalculated for that chip.

Cards brought by appraisal guild clients work the same way: pointing out problems changes the estimate until you report the correct value.
